lessons.unit: Unit 1: Paper 1 Section A - Reading literary fiction (Q1-Q3)
lessons.title: Reading fiction closely: Paper 1 and Question 1
objectives: Describe the structure and mark allocation of AQA Paper 1
Retrieve four accurate details for Question 1
Tell the difference between explicit information and inference

keywords.def: stated directly in the text
suggested but not stated; the reader has to work it out
a conclusion reached from clues in the text
putting a detail into your own words

starter: Name three word classes and give one example of each (for example: noun - mirror).
What is the difference between a simile and a metaphor? Give one of each about rain.
Why is it good adab to read instructions or a question fully before answering it?

teach.heading: Paper 1 at a glance
bullets: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing: 1 hour 45 minutes, 80 marks
Section A: reading one literary fiction extract, Questions 1-4, 40 marks
Section B: one piece of creative writing, Question 5, 40 marks
Spend about an hour on Section A and 45 minutes on Section B
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Show the five questions and their marks on screen: Q1 4 marks, Q2 8, Q3 8, Q4 20, Q5 40. Stress that Q4 and Q5 carry most marks. Ask: where should most of your time go? Many pupils over-spend on Q1 and Q2.

teach.heading: Question 1: list four things
bullets: Worth 4 marks: one mark for each correct detail
Use only the lines the question names
Short answers: a few words or a brief quotation is enough
No analysis here, so no marks for explaining effects
teach.note: Typical wording: 'List four things about the character from this part of the source.' Common error: copying a whole sentence or writing a paragraph. Remind pupils that a detail must be accurate to the lines given, not guessed.

teach.heading: Explicit and implicit
bullets: Explicit: the text says it outright
Implicit: the text hints and you infer
Example: 'He glanced at his watch' hints that he is impatient
Q1 mostly rewards explicit details; later questions reward inference
teach.note: Ask pupils what a person who keeps glancing at their watch might be feeling. Collect two or three inferences. Make the point that an inference must always be supported by something in the text, otherwise it is just a guess.

teach.heading: Worked example
bullets: Text: Nadia stands outside the school gates, bag clutched to her chest
Detail 1: it has stopped raining
Detail 2: she is counting lamp-posts
Detail 3: her brother has not come out yet
Detail 4: the caretaker is rattling keys
teach.note: Display the Nadia extract (see practice). Read it aloud, then model underlining four safe details. Show a rejected answer: 'Nadia is scared' (an inference, not stated). Ask pupils to say why it would not be safe for Q1.

teach.heading: Three reads, three jobs
bullets: Read 1: gist. Who, where, what is happening?
Read 2: detail. Underline facts, actions and descriptions
Read 3: effect. What mood or idea do the details build?
teach.note: This is the routine pupils will use every lesson of the course. Model it with a one-minute silent read. Ask what the 'mood' of the Nadia extract is and which words create it.

practice: Extract (read aloud): 'The rain had stopped but the pavement still shone like a long black mirror. Nadia stood outside the school gates with her bag clutched to her chest, counting the lamp-posts between her and home. Seven. Her little brother had not come out yet. Behind her, the caretaker rattled a bunch of keys and glanced at his watch.' Q1: List four things about Nadia or her surroundings from this extract.
Which of these are explicit and which implicit? (a) The rain had stopped. (b) The caretaker wants to lock up. (c) Nadia is worried about her brother.
independent: Extract: 'Omar's fingers drummed on the desk while the clock on the wall dragged itself towards four. Outside, the football field was a bright green rectangle, empty and waiting. He had finished the test twenty minutes ago and checked it twice; now he checked it a third time.' Write Q1: List four things about Omar or the classroom.
From the same extract, write two inferences about Omar, each starting 'This suggests that...' and each supported by a short quotation.
Write two sentences of your own, one containing an explicit detail and one a clue the reader must infer from.
exit: State one rule for answering Question 1 and one thing you must not do.
Rewrite 'Omar is bored and wants to go home' as an inference with a short quotation as evidence.
lessons.homework: Read a short story of your choice for 15 minutes and write down four explicit details and two inferences about the main character.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide the extract with line numbers and a word bank (drummed, dragged, checked); give sentence starters for inferences. Stretch: write an inference that links two separate details.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Paper 1 Section A - Reading literary fiction (Q1-Q3)
lessons.title: Question 2: analysing a writer's word choices
objectives: Explain what Question 2 asks and how it is marked
Zoom in on single words and explain their connotations
Write an analytical paragraph using terminology

keywords.def: the ideas or feelings a word suggests beyond its literal meaning
a word that shows an action or state
giving human qualities to something that is not human
explain how and why a writer's choices create an effect

starter: Define 'inference' and give one inference from: 'Omar checked his test a third time.'
Name the four things you can list for Question 1 from: 'The caretaker rattled his keys.'
What does the word 'crept' suggest that 'walked' does not?

teach.heading: What Question 2 asks
bullets: 8 marks, assessing AO2: language analysis
Focuses on a short named section of the source
Asks: how does the writer use language to describe something?
Aim for about 10 minutes and 2-3 well-developed points
teach.note: Show the question stem: 'How does the writer use language to describe the house?' Emphasise 'use language' means words and phrases, language features, techniques and sentence forms. Quality of analysis beats quantity of quotations.

teach.heading: Zoom in on one word
bullets: Choose a short quotation with a powerful word
Name its word class: verb, adjective, noun, adverb
Explain its connotations: what does it suggest?
Link to the overall mood or idea
teach.note: Display: 'The old house crouched at the end of the lane, its windows dark and watchful.' Ask: what does 'crouched' suggest about the house? Elicit: animal-like, ready to pounce, hiding, threatening. Tell pupils that the verb does the work, so zoom in on it.

teach.heading: Model paragraph
bullets: Point: the writer presents the house as menacing
Evidence: 'crouched at the end of the lane'
Analysis: the verb 'crouched' personifies the house as a predator
Effect: the reader feels watched and uneasy
teach.note: Read the full model: 'The writer presents the house as menacing from the start. The verb 'crouched' personifies it as an animal ready to pounce, suggesting it is waiting for visitors, which makes the reader feel uneasy before anything has happened.' Annotate point, evidence, analysis, effect in four colours.

teach.heading: Avoid these traps
bullets: Feature-spotting: 'this is a simile' earns very little
Vague effects: 'it makes the reader want to read on'
Retelling the story instead of analysing it
Always say what the technique suggests, and why
teach.note: Ask pupils to improve a weak sentence live: 'The writer uses a verb to make it interesting.' Push for which verb, what it suggests, and what the reader feels. Use the phrase 'What? How? Why?' as a prompt.

teach.heading: Try it together
bullets: Text: a cold wind dragged brittle leaves across the porch
Zoom in on 'dragged' and 'brittle'
Think: force, effort, fragility, decay
teach.note: Take suggestions and build a joint paragraph on screen. 'Dragged' implies the wind is forceful and the leaves helpless; 'brittle' suggests decay and fragility, matching the house's neglect.

practice: Text: 'The old house crouched at the end of the lane, its windows dark and watchful. A cold wind dragged brittle leaves across the porch, and somewhere inside a shutter banged like a slammed door.' Choose the word 'banged' and write a point-evidence-analysis-effect paragraph about it.
Improve this weak sentence: 'The writer uses an adjective, 'dark', and it creates an effect.'
independent: Write a full Q2-style paragraph on 'watchful' (hint: what human quality does it give the windows?).
Write a second paragraph on 'dragged' or 'brittle', using a different word class.
Self-check: underline in your answers (a) a quotation, (b) a word class, (c) a connotation, (d) an effect on the reader.
exit: Give two things that make a strong Question 2 paragraph.
Explain in one sentence what the verb 'crept' suggests in 'fog crept over the field'.
lessons.homework: Find a descriptive passage in any novel and write one analytical paragraph (point, evidence, analysis, effect) about a single word.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a frame ('The word ___ is a ___. It suggests ___, so the reader feels ___') and a connotation word bank. Stretch: compare two words of the same class and explain which is stronger.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Paper 1 Section A - Reading literary fiction (Q1-Q3)
lessons.title: Question 2: imagery, sentence forms and tone
objectives: Identify and explain similes, metaphors and personification
Comment on sentence length and form as a language choice
Combine word-level and sentence-level analysis in one answer

keywords.def: a group of words linked by a common theme
repeated 's' or 'sh' sounds
a short sentence with no main verb, used for effect
the attitude or mood the writer creates

starter: Define connotation and give the connotations of the word 'gripped'.
Write a metaphor and a simile for a noisy classroom.
Which of these is a minor sentence? 'Seven.' / 'She counted seven lamp-posts.'

teach.heading: Imagery that earns marks
bullets: Simile: compares using 'like' or 'as'
Metaphor: says one thing is another
Personification: human qualities given to non-human things
Always explain what the comparison makes us picture
teach.note: Bismillah and brief recap. Show: 'Stalls blossomed with colour' (metaphor/personification). Ask: why 'blossomed' not 'appeared'? Elicit growth, beauty, life. Stress that labelling is only the first step; the explanation earns the marks.

teach.heading: Semantic fields and sound
bullets: Semantic field: words from one theme build a picture
Market example: scarlet, golden, silver all suggest richness
Alliteration and sibilance affect pace and mood
Comment only when the sound clearly supports the meaning
teach.note: Display the market extract: 'The market roared into life at dawn. Stalls blossomed with colour: scarlet peppers, golden oranges, silver fish stacked like coins.' Ask pupils to find a semantic field (colour/wealth). Warn against forcing sound comments where they do not fit.

teach.heading: Sentence forms as choices
bullets: Short sentences can speed up action or add tension
Long sentences can slow time or build detail
Minor sentences give a sudden, striking beat
A list suggests abundance or overload
teach.note: Use the extract's 'Hawkers bellowed.' (short, loud) and the final comparison 'a sparrow among pigeons' (small, quick, easily lost). Ask what the short sentence does to the pace. Point out that sentence forms are also language, so they are allowed in Q2.

teach.heading: Tone and viewpoint
bullets: Tone: how the narrator feels about what is described
The market is lively and joyful but also crowded
Hassan as a small bird suggests he is vulnerable and nimble
Link each technique back to the question focus
teach.note: Ask: is the narrator admiring or fearful of the market? Evidence for both. This builds the nuanced reading needed for the higher levels.

teach.heading: Putting it together
bullets: Pick three strong quotations from different parts of the section
Mix word, technique and sentence-form comments
Write: Point, Evidence, Analysis, Effect for each
Keep the question focus in every paragraph
teach.note: Model planning on the board: three boxes (word, imagery, sentence). Time check: ten minutes for a real Q2. Take questions.

practice: Text: 'The market roared into life at dawn. Stalls blossomed with colour: scarlet peppers, golden oranges, silver fish stacked like coins. Hawkers bellowed. Hassan wove between them, small and quick, a sparrow among pigeons.' Explain in two sentences what 'roared' suggests about the market.
Explain what the short sentence 'Hawkers bellowed.' adds to the passage.
independent: Q2: How does the writer use language to describe the market? Write three PEAE paragraphs: one on a word, one on imagery, one on sentence form.
Rewrite the final sentence as a simile instead of a metaphor. Which is more effective and why?
Add a fourth paragraph on the colour words, naming the semantic field.
exit: Name one technique and explain its effect in 'stalls blossomed with colour'.
Why can a very short sentence be effective in descriptive writing?
lessons.homework: Write six descriptive sentences about your own street at dusk using one simile, one metaphor, one personification and one short sentence. Underline each technique.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a colour-coded model paragraph and a glossary with pictures for roared, bellowed, hawkers. Stretch: analyse how tone shifts between the first and last sentences.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Paper 1 Section A - Reading literary fiction (Q1-Q3)
lessons.title: Question 3: how writers structure a text
objectives: Explain what structure means in a fiction extract
Track shifts in focus, time and perspective
Write a structural paragraph with a clear effect on the reader

keywords.def: the way a writer organises and sequences a text
a change in what the writer concentrates on
moving from a wide view to a detail, or the reverse
ending in a way that echoes the beginning

starter: State two differences between language analysis (Q2) and structure analysis (Q3).
Give an example of a short sentence and say what it does to pace.
What does 'personification' mean? Give an example about a city.

teach.heading: What Question 3 asks
bullets: 8 marks, AO2: structural features
Covers the whole extract, not a short section
Typical wording: how has the writer structured the text to interest you?
Aim for about 10 minutes and 3-4 structural points
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Contrast with Q2: Q2 is about words and sentences in a section; Q3 is about the order of ideas across the whole text. Pupils often analyse words by mistake, which earns no marks in Q3.

teach.heading: Structural questions to ask
bullets: Where does the extract begin and why?
Where does the focus shift: person, place, time, mood?
Does it zoom in on a detail or pull back?
How does it end, and how does that link to the start?
teach.note: Write these four questions on the board and keep them there for the next three lessons. Model on the Omar extract: starts inside the room with the clock; widens to the empty field outside; ends on Omar's third check.

teach.heading: Worked example: Omar
bullets: Opens on small movement: fingers drumming, clock dragging
Pulls focus outward to the empty, waiting field
Returns to Omar and the repeated checking
Effect: the field tempts him, so the ending feels like frustration
teach.note: Read the extract again slowly. Draw a simple zoom diagram: inside, outside, back inside. Ask pupils what the contrast between the lively field and the stuck classroom creates. The cyclical return to checking suggests he is trapped.

teach.heading: Writing a structure paragraph
bullets: Name the structural feature and where it happens
Use a short quotation as evidence
Say what the shift does: build tension, contrast, reveal
Finish with the effect on the reader
teach.note: Model sentence frames on screen: 'The extract begins with... then shifts to... This contrast creates...' Emphasise 'then shifts to' language. Do not allow lists of features without effects.

teach.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Writing about word choices instead of order and focus
Saying 'the writer uses paragraphs' with no effect
Missing the ending or the very first sentence
teach.note: Take a weak answer ('The writer uses short and long sentences') and rebuild it into a structural point: why is the first paragraph short, and what does the last paragraph do?

practice: Extract (Omar, from Lesson 1). Write a paragraph beginning: 'The extract begins by focusing on...' and include one effect on the reader.
Draw a three-box timeline of the Nadia extract (opening, middle, end) and label where the focus shifts.
independent: Q3: How has the writer structured the Omar extract to interest you as a reader? Write two structural paragraphs.
Write the opening three sentences of a story where the focus zooms from a whole street to one closed window.
Annotate your own three sentences: label the zoom and the effect.
exit: Name two structural features you can comment on in Question 3.
What question should you ask about the ending of an extract?
lessons.homework: Choose the first page of a novel you know. Write three sentences describing how the focus moves from the first paragraph to the last.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide the timeline template pre-drawn and sentence frames. Stretch: identify a structural pattern across two paragraphs and evaluate its effect.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Paper 1 Section A - Reading literary fiction (Q1-Q3)
lessons.title: Question 3: tension, paragraphs and the shape of a story
objectives: Identify structural devices that build tension or reveal information
Comment on paragraph length and withholding information
Write a developed Q3 answer using several features

keywords.def: hinting at what will happen later
holding back a detail to build curiosity
a scene that shows an earlier time
an unresolved ending that leaves the reader waiting

starter: Name two questions you can ask about structure in an extract.
What is a shift in focus? Give an example.
Define cyclical structure.

teach.heading: Building tension
bullets: Short paragraphs speed up the pace
A one-line paragraph can land like a shock
Slow description can delay a fear or a reveal
Repetition can make a worry grow
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Ask: when does a film cut quickly, and why? Link this to short paragraphs. Show how the Nadia extract uses a single word sentence ('Seven.') to make us feel time dragging.

teach.heading: Withholding and foreshadowing
bullets: A writer may hide who is speaking or what is wrong
Small clues hint at later events
The reader reads on to fill the gap
Comment on what the gap makes us ask
teach.note: Display an opening: 'The phone rang. Nobody in the house moved.' Ask pupils what questions they now have. Emphasise that questions in the reader's mind are the structural effect.

teach.heading: Time and perspective
bullets: Flashback: pulls us into the past to explain the present
Change of perspective: another viewpoint or distance
Dialogue breaks narration and speeds the page
Ending: closed, open or twist
teach.note: Briefly show how a story might move from a character's hands trembling to a memory of a promise. The structural point is the movement, not just the content.

teach.heading: Model answer on a new extract
bullets: Opening: a ringing phone nobody answers
Middle: focus shifts to the hallway and a missing key
End: a short final line, 'It stopped.'
Effect: delay, then sudden silence makes us uneasy
teach.note: Teacher-written extract: 'The phone rang. Nobody in the house moved. In the hallway, the coat hooks held three coats and one empty hook where Dad's should have been. The ringing went on. Aisha counted the rings, eight, nine, ten. It stopped.' Walk through the structure: sound, then image, then counting, then silence.

teach.heading: Structure an answer
bullets: Start with the opening and why it hooks us
Then move through the shifts in order
Finish with the ending and its effect
Aim for four developed points
teach.note: Give pupils a three-part frame: beginning, middle, end. Remind them that Q3 marks reward linking features to how the reader is interested, so keep the word 'reader' in each paragraph.

practice: Using the phone extract on the slide, find two structural features and name the effect of each.
Explain why the single-word sentence 'Seven.' in the Nadia extract matters structurally.
independent: Q3: How has the writer structured the phone extract to interest you as a reader? Write three paragraphs.
Add a fourth paragraph on the ending 'It stopped.' and what it leaves the reader thinking.
Rewrite the opening so that it uses a flashback instead of a ringing phone.
exit: Give one structural way a writer can build tension.
What effect does withholding information have on the reader?
lessons.homework: Write a 120-word story opening that holds back one key piece of information and ends on a short sentence.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: supply a paragraph frame (The text begins... then... finally...) and glossary pictures for foreshadowing. Stretch: evaluate whether the ending is more effective as closed or open.

lessons.title: Question 4: evaluating a statement about a text
objectives: Understand what evaluate means in Question 4
Break a statement into ideas and test them against the text
Plan a balanced evaluation with evidence

keywords.def: judge how well something works, supported by evidence
a student's opinion that you must test
weighing up carefully rather than just agreeing
asks how far you agree, not just whether you do

starter: Name two structural features and explain one.
Explain what 'implicit' means.
Write a short sentence that builds suspense.

teach.heading: What Question 4 asks
bullets: 20 marks, AO4: evaluate critically
Focuses on the second half or final part of the source
A student's statement is given: to what extent do you agree?
Spend about 20 minutes
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Show a model stem: 'A student said: 'This part of the story shows the character is very afraid.' To what extent do you agree?' Remind pupils it is a 20-mark question and the biggest in Section A.

teach.heading: Unpack the statement
bullets: Underline the key idea: here, 'very afraid'
Ask: is this fully true, partly true, or hard to say?
Find evidence for and against, then decide
Your view needs a reason, not just a label
teach.note: Give a small extract (below) and ask pupils to find a quotation that suggests fear and one that suggests curiosity or calm. This shows that 'to some extent' answers are often the most convincing.

teach.heading: Evaluate, don't just describe
bullets: Describe: 'The writer says the stairs creaked'
Analyse: 'The verb 'creaked' suggests age and danger'
Evaluate: 'This is most effective because the sound grows'
Judge how well methods support the statement
teach.note: Ask pupils to rank three sentences from describing to evaluating. Make the point that evaluation uses phrases like 'this is effective because', 'the strongest example', 'although'.

teach.heading: Plan in four steps
bullets: Interpret the statement in your own words
Select 3-4 quotations from the specified part
Analyse methods and effects with terminology
Conclude with a clear, justified level of agreement
teach.note: Model a short plan on the board using the staircase extract (practice). Explain the final judgement: 'to a large extent' because three of four details point to fear, but one shows determination.

teach.heading: Useful evaluative language
bullets: I largely agree because...
However, the writer also suggests...
The most convincing evidence is...
Overall, the effect on the reader is...
teach.note: Give these stems out in the chat. Insist that every stem is followed by a quotation and analysis rather than only opinion.

practice: Extract: 'Sami climbed the stairs one step at a time. The wooden boards complained under his weight. At the top, the door was open a hand's width, and a thin line of yellow light lay across the carpet like a dropped ribbon. He swallowed, but his hand did not shake when he pushed it.' Statement: 'This part of the story shows that Sami is very afraid.' Find two quotations that support it and one that challenges it.
Write a one-sentence interpretation of the statement in your own words.
independent: Plan a Q4 answer to the statement about Sami using the four-step method.
Write the first evaluative paragraph agreeing in part, with a quotation and an analysis of one word.
Write a second paragraph that challenges the statement with the quotation about his hand.
exit: In one sentence, what does 'evaluate' mean in Q4?
Write an evaluative sentence stem you will use in your answer.
lessons.homework: Rewrite your plan as a complete paragraph that starts with 'I largely agree because...' and includes one quotation analysed in detail.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a two-column agree/disagree grid and a stem bank. Stretch: include a sentence on how the writer's structural choices support the judgement.

lessons.title: Question 4: writing a full evaluation
objectives: Write a developed 20-mark style response in timed conditions
Use embedded quotations and precise terminology
Self-assess against level descriptors

keywords.def: a short quotation woven into your own sentence
showing insight beyond the obvious
your reasoned view, built from evidence
technical language such as metaphor or semantic field

starter: List the four steps for planning Q4.
Rewrite as evaluation: 'The writer uses a metaphor in line 5.'
What does 'to what extent' ask you to do?

teach.heading: Recap the pathway
bullets: Interpret the statement
Select quotations from the named part
Analyse methods and effects
Judge how far you agree
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Remind pupils that Q4 is the highest-scoring reading question, and that practice with real timing matters. Show the examiner's focus: critical evaluation, supporting views with references.

teach.heading: Model paragraph
bullets: Claim: the writer builds fear through sound
Evidence: wooden boards 'complained under his weight'
Analysis: personification makes the house seem alive and hostile
Evaluation: effective because it makes each step feel risky
teach.note: Display the model paragraph in full. Ask pupils to underline claim, quotation, technique, effect and evaluative phrase. Highlight that the quotation is embedded in the sentence.

teach.heading: Level up your response
bullets: Use the writer's name or 'the writer' consistently
Develop fewer points in more depth
Address both sides of the statement
Close with a justified overall judgement
teach.note: Show a weaker paragraph that names techniques with no effect, and a stronger one. Ask pupils to say what makes it perceptive. Mention that conclusions should not simply restate the question.

teach.heading: Timing and layout
bullets: 2 minutes: re-read the named part
3 minutes: quick plan with four quotations
13 minutes: write four paragraphs
2 minutes: check quotations and spelling
teach.note: Pupils write in the independent section under these timings. Online setting: they type or write and photograph their work. Set the clock visibly.

practice: Use the Sami extract. Orally rehearse your opening sentence and the first quotation you would use.
Mark this sentence for quality: 'There is a simile and it is good.' What is missing?
independent: Timed (about 18 minutes): 'A student said: 'The writer makes Sami seem brave rather than afraid.' To what extent do you agree?' Write a full response using the Sami extract from Lesson 6.
Highlight your response: one colour for quotations, one for analysis, one for evaluation phrases.
Write one sentence to improve your own conclusion.
exit: Name one thing your answer did well and one target for next time.
Give one evaluative phrase you will reuse.
lessons.homework: Rewrite your weakest paragraph, adding a second quotation and a sentence of evaluation.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: allow a paragraph frame and extra time; chunk the task into two sittings. Stretch: weave in a comment on structure as well as language.

lessons.title: Description: planning from a prompt or image with the CLOSER lens
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a writer control what the reader sees?
objectives: To understand how to plan a descriptive piece that guides the reader's eye with one controlled viewpoint
successCriteria: All: turn a prompt or image into a five-part CLOSER plan

teach.heading: A 19th-century sentence

quote.text: Oh! But he was a tight-fisted hand at the grindstone, Scrooge! a squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching, covetous old sinner!
quote.source: Charles Dickens, A Christmas Carol (1843), Stave One (public domain)

teach.note: Read aloud slowly. Chunk it: 'he was a tight-fisted hand at the grindstone' = he squeezed every penny out of work. Cultural context: this is from Charles Dickens, A Christmas Carol (1843), set in Victorian London where a few were rich and many were very poor. Scrooge is a moneylender. 'Grindstone' is a heavy stone wheel used to sharpen tools: a hand pressed against it is hurt, so the metaphor shows Scrooge making people suffer. Public domain.

teach.heading: Worked model: decode then analyse

model.problem: What effect does Dickens create with the list 'squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching, covetous'?
steps: Decode: the sentence describes Scrooge as a greedy man who takes everything he can.
Method: a list of six present participles ('-ing' words), then one adjective.
Meaning: each verb is a harsh physical action, so Scrooge seems to be physically tearing money from people.
Effect: the piling-up of verbs creates a breathless, relentless rhythm, so the reader feels how greedy and cruel he is.
Zoom: 'covetous' ends the list as a final, judging word, which turns the description into a moral condemnation.
model.answer: Dickens uses an escalating list of harsh verbs to make Scrooge's greed feel relentless and physical. The final word 'covetous' passes moral judgement on him, so the reader is prepared to dislike him from the start.

teach.note: Walk through each step on the board before pupils try. Point out the whole answer is only four sentences; length is not the goal, precision is. EAL support: write 'covetous = wanting what belongs to others' beside the quote.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which comment best explains the effect of the list of verbs?

It shows how greedy and harsh Scrooge is, and the rhythm feels relentless.
It shows Scrooge likes working with tools.
check.why: B links the method (list) to effect and meaning. A is not supported by the text; C takes 'grindstone' literally and ignores the metaphor.

teach.note: Pupils answer on mini-whiteboards. Confirm B, then ask why A and C are tempting: pupils often choose the answer that sounds most 'literary' rather than the one that is supported by evidence.

teach.heading: Meet the extract

quote.text:
1 Rain had been falling on Dunmere bus station since lunchtime.
2 Under the metal shelter, a woman in a yellow raincoat sat with a
3 cardboard box on her knees, holding it as if it might escape.
4 Beside her, a boy of about twelve swung his school bag against the
5 bench: thud, thud, thud. A broken timetable flapped on its hook.
6 The 4.40 to Harbury was already twenty minutes late.
7 Nobody spoke. A pigeon walked between their feet, unbothered.
quote.source: Original extract written for TGA

teach.note: Read it aloud while pupils follow the line numbers. Cultural context: this is an ordinary British bus station in rain; 'the 4.40' uses the 12-hour clock without 'pm'; buses often run late and a timetable is a printed list of times. 'Unbothered' = not worried. This is an original text written for this lesson.

teach.heading: The Question 1 routine
cycle: Read the question: note the line numbers
Write each as a short quotation or paraphrase
teach.note: Say: this is the quickest question on the paper, but pupils throw marks away by drifting outside the named lines. Model with a finger on line numbers. Remind them that four marks means four separate details; two details from one sentence still count as two if distinct.

teach.heading: Worked model answer

model.problem: List four things from lines 1 to 6 about the bus station and the people waiting there.
steps: Read lines 1-6 only and number each fact you find.
Fact 1: it has been raining since lunchtime.
Fact 2: a woman wears a yellow raincoat and holds a cardboard box on her knees.
Fact 3: a boy of about twelve swings his school bag against the bench.
Fact 4: the 4.40 bus to Harbury is twenty minutes late (the timetable is broken).
model.answer: Four marks: rain since lunchtime; woman in yellow raincoat with box; boy about twelve swinging bag; bus twenty minutes late.

teach.note: Show that each point is a single, different detail. Note the answer also avoids saying the woman is 'sad' or the box is 'a kitten', which is inference not stated in the lines.

teach.heading: Common mistakes

misconception.wrong: 'The woman is anxious because she holds the box tightly and the bus is late.' (inference from lines 2-6)
misconception.right: 'A woman holds a cardboard box on her knees.' (an explicit detail that can be quoted or paraphrased)

teach.note: Ask pupils to spot which answer in a class set would earn fewer marks and why. Link to AO1: the question tests explicit retrieval, while implicit meaning is tested in other questions.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which is a valid fourth detail for 'lines 1 to 6'?
options: A pigeon walked between their feet.
The bus to Harbury was twenty minutes late.
The woman was waiting for her son.
check.why: B is stated in line 6. A is line 7, outside the range. C is not in the text.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. Answer is B. The trap in A is using line 7, outside the named lines; C is an invented detail.

practice: Using lines 1-7 of the extract, list four things about the boy, the woman or the pigeon, without repeating a detail.

teach.heading: The extract

quote.text: Before the sun had properly arrived, the market was already shouting. Stallholders hurled crates onto trestle tables with a crash that rattled the pavement. The air was thick with the sweet, rotting smell of oranges and the sharp tang of fish ice. A man with a face like creased leather roared prices at nobody in particular, while the pale light crept over the rooftops like a nervous cat.
quote.source: Original extract written for TGA

teach.note: Read with expression. Explain 'trestle table' (a folding market table) and 'stallholder' (a person who sells at a market stall). Cultural context: open-air street markets are common in British towns, often starting very early. This is an original extract.

teach.heading: The method: Q-M-E-Z
cycle: Method: name the technique or word class
Effect: what it suggests and how the reader feels
Zoom: one single word within the quote
teach.note: Explain the four steps on the board and tell pupils the bullets on the paper are guidance only; they carry no marks. Ask: why is naming a technique alone not enough? Draw out that examiners reward effect and perceptive exploration.

teach.heading: Worked model: a Level 4 paragraph

model.problem: How does the writer use language to describe the market at dawn? (8 marks)
steps: Quote and method: the personification 'the market was already shouting' gives the place an aggressive human voice.
Effect: it suggests an impatient, noisy place that never rests, so the reader feels overwhelmed.
Zoom: 'already' implies the day has barely started yet the market is up to full volume.
Second quote: the verb 'hurled' has connotations of violence and carelessness, reinforced by the onomatopoeic 'crash'.
Contrast: the simile 'like a nervous cat' makes the sunrise tentative, so the gentle light seems to intrude on the market's roughness.
model.answer: The writer personifies the market from the outset: it 'was already shouting', which gives it an aggressive human voice and suggests an impatient place that never rests. The adverb 'already' implies the day has hardly begun and yet the noise is at full volume, overwhelming the reader. The verb 'hurled' in 'hurled crates' connotes carelessness and energy, and the onomatopoeic 'crash' reinforces the harsh soundscape. In contrast, the simile 'like a nervous cat' makes the dawn light tentative and delicate, so it seems to intrude on a rough, noisy world. This contrast makes the market feel vivid and slightly intimidating.

teach.note: Read the model, then ask pupils to underline each step in different colours. Point out the zoom words, 'hurled' and 'already', and the contrast structure. Say it is about 120 words, a realistic timed length. Ask: where does the writer say 'the writer uses' without effect? None.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which sentence is closest to Level 4 analysis?
options: 'The writer uses a simile, which is a technique.'
'The writer says the light crept over the rooftops.'
'The simile "like a nervous cat" makes the dawn light seem timid, contrasting with the loud, rough market.'
check.why: C names the method, quotes it, and explains the effect and the contrast. A has no effect; B only retells the text.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is C. Discuss why A and B score low: A names the technique but gives no effect; B only describes.

teach.heading: Common error

misconception.wrong: 'The writer uses a metaphor and an adjective and a verb to make it interesting.'
misconception.right: 'The adjective "creased" in "creased leather" suggests the man's face is weathered and tough, so the reader sees him as a hardened trader.'

teach.note: Run a quick pair talk on which version the examiner would credit. Support EAL pupils with the sentence stem on the right.

practice: Write one Q-M-E-Z sentence on 'the sweet, rotting smell of oranges'.

exit: What does Q-M-E-Z stand for?

Big question: what separates perceptive analysis from technique-spotting?

lessons.title: Question 4: modelling an evaluative answer to a statement
lessons.bigQuestion: How do I weigh a statement and still give a clear personal judgement?
objectives: Read a Question 4 statement and plan a balanced judgement
Write an evaluative paragraph with a quotation, a method and a reader response
Use evaluative stems to show 'to what extent' the statement is true
successCriteria: All: agree or disagree with a statement using evidence

keywords.def: make a judgement about how well something works, using evidence
how far you agree with a statement
a reasoned opinion supported by quotation
how the reader feels or what they imagine
the opinion in the question that you must test

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: name two structural features of the Tarn End extract.
Rewrite 'I think it is good' as an evaluative sentence with evidence.
What is the difference between 'describe' and 'evaluate'?

teach.heading: The Question 4 statement

quote.text: A student said: 'This extract makes waiting feel unbearable. The writer uses Safiya's thoughts and short sentences to make me feel her fear.' To what extent do you agree? (20 marks)
quote.source: Original question written for TGA

teach.note: Use the Tarn End extract from the previous lesson (reprint it for pupils). Ask pupils to decide where they stand on a 0-10 line. Tell them there is no right side; marks reward the quality of the evaluation. Warn that 'to what extent' invites 'mostly agree' or 'partly agree', not a simple yes or no.

teach.heading: Plan: agree, test, judge
cycle: Agree: where is the statement true? Give evidence.
Test: where might it be less true or too simple?
Methods: which language and structure choices support it?
Judge: how far do you agree? State clearly.
teach.note: Walk through the plan and note that you evaluate the statement, not just the text. Remind them that Q4 focuses on a stated part, usually the second half of the extract, in the real paper; here we use the whole of Tarn End for practice. Stress paragraph structure: point, quotation, method, effect, evaluation.

teach.heading: Worked model: an evaluative paragraph

model.problem: To what extent do you agree that the writer makes the reader feel Safiya's fear?
steps: Agree: use 'the creak of the stairs that did not come' to show the waiting is tense.
Method: the list 'the clock, the kettle, the creak' piles up small sounds and makes time feel slow.
Evaluate: it is not only fear, because 'her brother's coat still hung on the hook' suggests longing.
Judge: the statement is mostly true but incomplete, because grief is as strong as fear.
model.answer: I largely agree that the writer makes the reader feel Safiya's fear. The list 'the clock, the kettle, the creak of the stairs that did not come' piles up tiny sounds, so time feels slow and the silence menacing. Yet the statement overlooks how much of the tension is sadness: 'her brother's coat still hung on the hook' implies she is longing for someone who is absent. The short sentences 'A gate. Footsteps, slow, crunching.' do raise fear, but they are as much hope as dread, because she is waiting for him. The reader therefore feels a mixture of fear and longing, so the statement is mostly accurate but too simple.

teach.note: Annotate the model for evaluative verbs ('partly', 'although', 'more than'). Point out the writer takes a position, does not just tell the story. Ask pupils where the writer shifts from agreeing to refining the opinion.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which sentence best shows 'to what extent'?
options: 'I agree because the writer is good.'
'I disagree because it is not scary.'
'I mostly agree, but the statement overlooks the sadness in the coat on the hook.'
check.why: C weighs the statement and refines it with evidence. A and B give a simple verdict and no evidence.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is C. Pupils sometimes believe they must fully disagree to show critical thinking; remind them agreement can be perceptive too.

teach.heading: Evaluation vocabulary
bullets: largely, partly, to some extent
however, although, whereas
more than, rather than
this suggests, this implies
teach.note: Give EAL pupils the list and have them use two in a sentence. Say that Q4 asks about the writer's methods and the reader's response, so each point needs both.

practice: Write the first sentence of a Q4 answer that agrees partly with the statement.
Find one quotation in paragraphs 3-6 that supports the statement and name its method.

Extend: Write two paragraphs, one agreeing and one refining, plus a one-line conclusion.
Stretch: Write a full 250-word Q4 response with an introduction, two paragraphs and a conclusion.
exit: Write one evaluative stem you will use.
Why is 'I agree' without a quotation weak?
Big question: finish 'To weigh a statement, I ...'

EAL/international: pre-teach 'unbearable', 'menacing', 'longing', 'overlooks', 'refines'; idiom 'to read between the lines' = to notice what is not stated; stems: 'I partly agree because ...', 'However, the writer also ...', 'This makes the reader feel ...'. Cultural note: UK exams often ask pupils to give a reasoned opinion; no single answer is correct. Stretch: argue the opposite view of the statement convincingly.

Add a stance: closing early harms pupils.

teach.heading: Text C: A Night in the Dunes
teach.note: Teacher-written travel writing. Read twice: once for meaning, once with a pen.

quote.text: By the time we reached the dunes, the heat had drained from the sand like water from a basin. Our guide said nothing; he simply pointed upward. I have seen city skies and mountain skies, but nothing prepared me for this: a sky so crowded with stars that the darkness seemed the exception.

model.problem: What does the guide's silence suggest?
steps: Explicit: 'Our guide said nothing'
Clue: he 'simply pointed upward'
Inference: the view needs no words; he knows it is extraordinary
Write: Point + brief quotation + inference
model.answer: The guide's silence ('said nothing') implies the sky is so remarkable that words would only diminish it.

check.q: Which is an inference rather than retrieval?

The writer is used to busy, light-polluted places.
check.why: It is not stated; it is drawn from 'city skies' and 'the darkness seemed the exception'.

independent.model: Inference question model: 'What does "crowded with stars" suggest?' Answer: It suggests an overwhelming number of stars, so many that the sky feels full, showing the writer's astonishment.

independent.q: Stretch: infer something about the writer's normal life.

Technique: simile
Zoom: 'drained' suggests emptying completely

check.q: Which sentence lets effect lead?

independent.model: Point: The writer presents the night sky as overwhelming in its beauty. | Evidence: 'a sky so crowded with stars that the darkness seemed the exception' | Technique: hyperbole and inversion of expectation | Zoom in: 'exception' reverses the normal idea that night is dark. | Analyse: The reader shares the writer's astonishment at a sky where light, not dark, is normal. | Alternative: It could also suggest how much the writer has been missing in brightly lit cities. | Link: So language makes the sky feel like a revelation.

teach.heading: What Question 4 really tests
bullets: A statement about the text is printed in the question
You judge how far you agree, citing evidence
The question carries 20 marks
Evaluation is marked on quality, not on which side you pick
teach.note: State the key point twice: you cannot 'fail' by disagreeing. A pupil who disagrees with strong evidence and explanation will score as highly as one who agrees. Ask: why would examiners design it this way? (Because AO4 is about critical judgement.) The statement usually focuses on a part of the text, so pupils should stay within the lines given.

teach.heading: The extract and statement

quote.text: Statement: 'The writer makes Maya seem very brave.' Evidence from the extract: She walked towards the black water, though her hands were trembling. 'I am not afraid,' she whispered, and did not believe a word of it.
quote.source: Original extract and statement written for TGA

teach.note: Read together. Elicit initial gut reactions: agree, disagree or partly. Emphasise that both brave (she walks forward) and afraid (trembling, whispered) are in the same lines, so strong answers can use both.

teach.heading: Model: two high-quality answers, opposite views

left.title: Agree (mostly)
points: 'she walked towards the black water' shows decisive action
The determination is clear even while 'her hands were trembling'
Bravery here means acting despite fear

right.title: Disagree (partly)
points: 'did not believe a word of it' shows Maya lies to herself
She seems frightened, so brave is too simple

teach.note: Both positions can reach the top level because each uses precise quotation, explains how the writer creates the impression and gives a reasoned judgement. Ask pupils to find the strongest piece of evidence on each side. Emphasise 'to what extent' invites a nuanced view in the middle.

teach.heading: Worked paragraph

model.problem: 'The writer makes Maya seem very brave.' To what extent do you agree? (20 marks, one paragraph)
steps: State your view clearly and with a degree: 'I partly agree.'
Choose a quotation that supports it and explain the writer's method.
Choose a quotation that complicates it and explain the effect.
Reach a judgement that weighs the two.
model.answer: I partly agree that Maya seems brave. She 'walked towards the black water', and the verb 'walked' shows she is moving forward, not running away. However, the writer undercuts this with 'her hands were trembling', which makes her fear physical and visible. The final clause, 'did not believe a word of it', shows she is trying to persuade herself, so her bravery seems effortful rather than natural. Overall, the writer presents courage as acting despite fear, which makes Maya more convincing and human than a fearless hero.

teach.note: Highlight the sequence: view, evidence, method, effect, weighing, judgement. Ask: where does it say 'I agree' or 'I disagree'? Only once, at the start. The rest is evaluation. Praise a model that changes mind within the paragraph, because that is critical.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: A pupil strongly disagrees with the statement and gives three well-explained quotations. What is the best prediction of their mark?
options: Low, because the statement should be supported
High, because the evaluation is strong
Impossible to tell until you check the position
check.why: Marks are for the quality of the evaluation. Disagreement is fully acceptable if supported by evidence and analysis.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. If some pick A, ask: what would the examiner be rewarding? Redirect to the quality of evaluation: evidence, method, effect, judgement.

practice: Write a one-sentence view on the statement, using a degree such as 'partly', 'mostly' or 'completely'.
Select the best quotation to oppose your view and say what it suggests.
Finish: 'Overall, the writer presents Maya as ... because ...'
independent: Core: Write a four-sentence evaluative paragraph that agrees partly.
Extend: Write a second paragraph that argues the opposite view, using different quotations.
Stretch: Write a conclusion that explains why neither view is complete, linking to the writer's purpose.
exit: True or false: you must agree with the statement to score highly.
Write one sentence beginning 'I partly agree because ...'.
Big question: how is the position you take marked?
lessons.homework: Take a statement about a character in a book you know, for example 'The writer makes the hero seem selfish'. Write one paragraph arguing for, and one against, then decide which you prefer.

EAL/international: pre-teach 'undercut', 'trembling', 'determination', 'convincing'; allow a bilingual vocabulary list. Stretch: write one paragraph which changes position half way and explain why the change is valid.

teach.note: Explain that Subject Content for writing expects pupils to use rhetorical and creative techniques for impact across both papers. Techniques overlap: a motif can persuade; a rhetorical question can build suspense. Ask: where have you seen the rule of three in advertising?

teach.heading: A public-domain model

quote.text: ... government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth.
quote.source: Abraham Lincoln, Gettysburg Address (1863)

teach.note: Point out the repeated 'of the people, by the people, for the people', which is both anaphora and a tricolon. This is public-domain text. Ask: what does the repetition make the audience feel? (Unity, dignity, rhythm.) Note it is a speech, so the sound matters.

teach.heading: Model: from plain to powerful

model.problem: Rewrite for impact for a school assembly speech on kindness: 'We should be kind to each other at school.'
steps: Add a rhetorical question that makes the audience reflect.
Use a tricolon to build rhythm.
Add direct address so the audience feels included.
End on a short, memorable sentence.
model.answer: Who here has never needed a kind word? Kindness costs us nothing: a smile, a shared seat, a gentle hello. You hold that power every single day. Use it.

teach.note: Break down each sentence aloud: the question, the tricolon (a smile, a shared seat, a gentle hello), the direct address 'You', the imperative 'Use it.' Ask pupils to read it as an assembly, feeling the impact. Original model written for TGA.

teach.heading: Creative impact in narrative

model.problem: Open a narrative using a motif and an extended metaphor. Subject: waiting for results.
steps: Pick a repeated image: a clock.
Build a metaphor in 2 to 3 sentences.
Use one very short sentence for emphasis.
Return to the motif at the end.
model.answer: The clock on the wall was a patient judge. Each tick weighed another minute against me. Tick. Tick. Outside, the corridor filled with footsteps, and the judge went on ticking.

teach.note: Name the motif (the clock), the extended metaphor (judge) and the fragment 'Tick. Tick.' as a deliberate short sentence. Stress that the ending returns to the clock, which delivers cohesion. Original model written for TGA.

check.why: Controlled use of one motif plus a short sentence creates a deliberate effect; piling on techniques weakens impact.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. Introduce 'less is more': one technique used well beats a list used badly.

model.problem: How does the writer use language and structure to show what the climb meant to her?
steps: Language: the counting 'twenty, then rest' mirrors her laboured breathing
Effect: the reader feels the effort in the rhythm
Structure: the anticlimax of 'only cloud' then the turn 'And yet'

model.answer: The counted rhythm of 'twenty, then rest' makes us feel her effort, and the structural turn from the anticlimax of 'only cloud' to 'And yet' shifts the meaning from the view to the achievement: she 'had earned the silence'.

model.problem: Compare how the two writers present reaching the top
steps: Similarity: both find the summit is not what they expected

Text Two: the valley 'like a map unrolled', met with tears
